g11-geography-ug5-t1.overview: Effects of Geographic Location on Development sits inside Geography and Economic Development. Geographic location is the focus of Unit 5 of Grade 11 Geography in the Ethiopian (FDRE Ministry of Education) curriculum. First, it weighs how geographic location shapes farming, industry, and services through the classic theories of von Thünen, Weber, and Christaller. Then it links climate extremes to poverty, sets out the trade hurdles that landlocked states such as Ethiopia face, and reviews intraregional trade in Africa, before leading into Unit 6: Major Global Environmental Changes. Students will also learn how geographic location applies to real-life situations.
objectives: Define economic growth and development and read the HDI.
Contrast geographic determinism with possibilism.
Explain how geographic location shapes agriculture, industry, and settlement.
Analyse how climate extremes deepen poverty and create poverty traps.
Describe the trade disadvantages that landlocked countries face.
g11-geography-ug5-t1.simple:
Effects of Geographic Location on Development in plain words. The exam wants you to recognise the core ideas, not to memorise whole paragraphs. Focus on:
  • First, the gap between economic growth and human development on the HDI scale.
  • The clash between geographic determinism and possibilism.
  • Then von Thünen’s rings, Weber’s least-cost triangle, and Christaller’s central places.
  • Finally, how each theory ties location to farming, industry, and service centres.

g11-geography-ug5-t3.simple:
Disadvantages of Landlocked Countries in plain words. The exam wants you to recognise the core ideas, not to memorise whole paragraphs. Focus on:
  • First, why landlocked states sit inland with no seacoast of their own.
  • The high transport costs that raise import prices and weaken exports.
  • Then dependence on transit neighbours’ roads, borders, and politics.
  • Finally, Ethiopia’s reliance on Djibouti and the search for other routes.

g11-geography-ug5-t4.simple:
Intraregional Trade in Africa in plain words. The exam wants you to recognise the core ideas, not to memorise whole paragraphs. Focus on:
  • First, how trade flows within Africa through RECs such as SADC and COMESA.
  • The top exporters and importers, led by South Africa.
  • Then the commodity mix, from staple foods to tea, coffee, and cotton.
  • Finally, the tariff and non-tariff barriers that slow African integration.
